analysis.one_liner: Raises merger filing fees on big deals, funds antitrust enforcement, and requires studies of merger effects on competition and wages.
analysis.headline: The Merger Enforcement Improvement Act was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a vote or hearing in the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise filing fees on very large mergers (up to $2.25 million for deals of $5 billion or more), use that money to fund the FTC and the Justice Department's antitrust division, and require companies that settle antitrust cases to report for five years on whether promised benefits like lower prices actually materialized. It also directs the FTC to study whether big institutional investors owning stakes in rival companies dampen competition, and directs the Government Accountability Office to study how mergers affect wages, employment, innovation, and new business formation.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers and workers gain from better-funded antitrust enforcement and better information: filing fees on giant mergers bankroll the agencies that police them, and the GAO studies would document how mergers affect wages and jobs. Small and mid-sized businesses competing against increasingly concentrated industries also gain from stronger enforcement.

how_it_helps.text: Raises filing fees on very large mergers — up to $2,250,000 for deals of $5 billion or more, with new tiers for deals above $1 billion and $2 billion — while lowering the fee for the smallest tier of covered deals to $30,000 and adjusting thresholds for inflation, and directs the extra revenue toward antitrust enforcement resources [S3].

Requires companies that settle antitrust cases with the FTC or Justice Department to report annually for five years on pricing, product quality, claimed efficiencies, and whether divestitures actually preserved competition — closing a gap where agencies never verified promised merger benefits [S3].
Directs the FTC, with the SEC, to study how much institutional investors own stakes in competing companies in concentrated markets and whether that overlapping ownership reduces competition [S3].

Directs the GAO to study whether merger remedies have actually worked, and to study the impact of mergers and acquisitions on wages, employment, innovation, and new business formation — the first systematic federal accounting of how consolidation affects paychecks [S3].
Authorizes $180.6 million for the Justice Department's Antitrust Division and $342 million for the FTC for fiscal year 2020 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations pursuing mergers pay substantially higher filing fees (up to $2.25 million) and, if they settle antitrust cases, face five years of mandatory reporting on pricing and promised efficiencies. Institutional investors whose funds hold shares in rival companies would face scrutiny from the FTC study.

drawbacks.text: Filing fees are a real cost of doing deals, and critics of merger fees argue they can deter some pro-competitive acquisitions, not just harmful ones — the bill lowers the smallest-tier fee but adds new fees of $400,000 to $2,250,000 for deals above $1 billion [S3].

The bill leans heavily on studies rather than new legal standards: the FTC study of common ownership and the GAO studies of remedies and wages would produce reports, not directly change enforcement, and past agency studies have not always led to action [S3].
Mandatory five-year post-settlement reporting imposes ongoing compliance costs on companies that settle with antitrust enforcers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall almost entirely on large companies attempting mergers, in the form of fees and reporting requirements, while the benefits — better-funded enforcement, verified merger remedies, and hard data on how consolidation affects wages and prices — accrue broadly to consumers and workers. The bill's main weakness is that it strengthens the information base for enforcement more than enforcement itself: it adds no new legal standards for blocking mergers, and its studies could go unused.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Klobuchar introduced the bill on January 31, 2019, and it was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill with eight original cosponsors — seven Democrats and independent Senator Angus King — on January 31, 2019 [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary that same day [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any other action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large companies pursuing mergers are better off: they face no new fees, no post-settlement reporting, and no new studies of how consolidation affects wages and competition, and antitrust enforcement resources remain as they were.

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters were Democrats or one independent (Angus King); no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Large corporations pursuing mergers and acquisitions
industries.note: The bill would raise their filing fees to as much as $2.25 million per mega-deal and require five years of post-settlement reporting if they settle an antitrust case. Their interest in avoiding these costs runs against the public's interest in merger scrutiny being funded and merger promises being verified.

The bill would require an FTC study of overlapping ownership — the practice of funds holding stakes in competing companies in the same concentrated market — using compulsory process. A study alone imposes no rules, but it targets a practice critics say quietly raises prices, and the industry would bear the scrutiny.

industries.industry: Antitrust enforcement agencies (DOJ Antitrust Division and FTC)
industries.note: The bill authorizes roughly $523 million combined for the two antitrust enforcement agencies for fiscal 2020, funded partly by the higher merger fees, expanding their capacity to challenge anticompetitive deals.

industries.industry: Antitrust bar and merger advisory firms (law firms, investment banks)
industries.note: Higher fees and more reporting raise deal costs, but better-funded enforcement and detailed post-settlement data create new advisory and compliance work for firms that specialize in mergers.
